article.title: Receive delivery receipts
article.excerpt: The platform POSTs to a URL you configure, with a token you generate. Two implementation details decide whether you lose events.

p: Configure the callback URL and generate the callback token in the console, then expose an endpoint that accepts a JSON POST. The platform posts when a message reaches a terminal state.
Each request carries an X-Callback-Token header. Verify it server-side before trusting the body.

steps.p: Console → Settings → Webhook. Use an HTTPS endpoint that is reachable from the public internet.
The token is what proves a request came from the platform. Store it server-side, not in client code.
Accept a JSON POST, verify the header, then acknowledge with a 2xx response.

head: Field
Meaning
rows: Platform message ID — your de-duplication key
delivered or failed, and nothing else
The provider's own wording, e.g. Twilio delivered or Vonage expired
Recipient and the provider that carried it
When the platform pushed it, ISO-8601 UTC

p: A non-2xx response, or a timeout, is retried on a 1s / 5s / 15s backoff, three times. After that the platform gives up and records the delivery as failed.
That retry behavior means you can legitimately receive the same event twice. De-duplicate on messageId rather than assuming exactly-once delivery.
list: Return 2xx only after you have durably accepted the event, not before.
Do not do slow work inline — a callback endpoint that takes seconds is a callback endpoint that gets retried.

sections.h: Which messages you will not hear about
p: Suppressed messages produce no callback. They were never handed to a provider, so delivered and failed do not apply — the outcome was fixed at acceptance.
